newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asian grain trade sees little impact from Deng.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian grain trade sees little impact from Deng.

text.p: Southeast Asia's grains and oilseeds business shrugged its shoulders on Thursday and ignored the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, regional traders said.
The market is more focused on open positions in April for buyers in Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for small cargoes of soymeal, they said.

"The reality is that it would be business as usual," a senior dealer for a U.S. commodity trading house told Reuters when asked whether Deng's death will affect China's behaviour in the grains and oilseeds market.
Another trader for a North American commodity firm said that China may become "pretty quiet for a while to take stock after Deng's death."
"If there is any impact, it will be very, very short-term. Everybody was expecting him to die soon anyway," the chief oilseeds dealer for a European trading company added.
Singapore-based traders said Chinese corn exports, which have been trickling out in small quantities, will not be affected by the passing away of Deng.
"The Chinese corn is coming out. I don't think his death will pose any problems," one U.S. trader said.
Regional firms are turning their attention to the small cargoes of soymeal that may be bought by Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand over the next few weeks, traders said.

Malaysia is believed to be interested in 5,000-10,000 tonnes of soymeal for April/June delivery, Indonesia for up to 20,000 tonnes of meal for May/July, and Thailand for 1,000 to 5,000 tonnes also in May/July, they said.
"The amount of business is really very small and on a hand-to-mouth basis," one trader said. "It's not really something to get excited about."
Southeast Asian remains thin as regional buyers have been driven to the sidelines by the recent sharp rise in Chicago futures prices.
"The amount of business is zero. These high prices have put everybody on the sidelines," a commodity house trader said.
"The destination markets are flooded with soybeans and soymeal. I don't really see any big demand coming out. Things have been very slow. People are just watching the market," another dealer said.

The long Chinese Lunar New Year and the Moslem Hari Raya holidays sidelined many people in the trade. The two holidays were celebrated from February 7-9, but most people took an extra week off and have just begun trickling back into their offices.
"People have been very slow coming back," one dealer said.
Quotes for corn, soybeans and soymeal in Southeast Asia have firmed in line with the recent rise in U.S. prices.

U.S. soybean prices coming into Southeast Asia were seen by regional dealers at around US$329-$330 a tonne C&F for April/May shipment on board a Panamax vessel against $316-$320 a tonne C&F last week.
Quotations for U.S. soymeal hovered around $320-$325 a tonne C&F for the same shipment period on a Panamax against $315-$317 a tonne C&F last week, dealers said.

Indian-origin soymeal, in comparison, was quoted at $314-$316 a tonne C&F for March/April delivery on a Tweendecker while a Handy-size shipment of Brazilian meal for April/May was quoted as low as $305 a tonne C&F, they said.
"People here are taking a close look at South American origin meal because of the price differential with the United States," one dealer said.
The same situation can be seen in the corn market.
U.S. corn coming into the region was quoted by dealers at around US$147-$150 a tonne C&F for April/May shipment on a Panamax against $145-$150 the previous week.
Argentine-origin corn for the same shipment was at $145 a tonne C&F, traders said.
